out.rationale: Arnesen et al. say they focus only on reading comprehension with an information-access expertise gap. Rahman et al. report debate beats consultancy by 4-10% for human judges on COVID-19 and climate claims; debaters are prompted GPT-4o, not trained, and judges are humans, not an LLM.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate helps judges outside reading comprehension, for COVID-19 and climate factuality claims

open_obligations: Note that the protocol is not recursive and debaters are not trained to equilibrium.

out.other_title: Open empirical questions: does debate help, reach equilibrium, show obfuscation?
out.rationale: Buhl et al. note most debate experiments use QuALITY with simple low-depth protocols and ask whether debate measurably improves performance and what systematic errors humans make. Rahman et al. report debate improves human accuracy and calibration over consultancy on COVID-19 and climate claims, with smaller gains for skeptical-prior judges; protocols are three-round prompted GPT-4o debates, not trained recursive debate.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate measurably improves human judgement outside QuALITY, for contested scientific claims

out.other_title: Limited setting: fiction QA, no strong judge priors, narrow information-only expertise gap
out.rationale: Michael et al. say debate is untested on political or ideologically charged issues and with judges holding strong priors. Rahman et al. test COVID-19 and climate claims with human judges screened for mainstream or skeptical beliefs and report debate beats consultancy by 4-10%; debaters are GPT-4o with curated sources rather than expert humans.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate's advantage over consultancy holds on ideologically charged claims with judges holding strong priors

open_obligations: Note that Rahman et al.'s baseline is consultancy, while Parrish et al. compare with no arguments.

out.other_title: Could debate help human judges in other set-ups such as highly technical tasks?
out.rationale: Parrish et al. conclude debate may help in other set-ups, such as highly technical tasks, though not for multiple-choice reading comprehension. Rahman et al. report that on COVID-19 and climate-change factuality claims, debate between GPT-4o agents improves human judges' accuracy and calibration and beats consultancy by 4-10%; the comparison is with consultancy, not with a no-argument condition as in Parrish et al., and the claims are scientific but not highly technical.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate helps human judges in set-ups other than multiple-choice reading comprehension, here contested scientific factuality claims

text: The paper studies whether debate between two AI systems on controversial COVID-19 and climate-change factuality claims guides judges with strong prior beliefs toward the truth, comparing debate with single-advisor consultancy for human judges with mainstream or skeptical beliefs (Study I) and for AI judges with and without personas (Study II). It reports that in Study I debate improves human accuracy and calibration, beating consultancy by 4-10% across the two domains, most for mainstream-belief judges (up to +15.2% on COVID-19), with +4.7% for skeptical judges.
title: AI debate helps biased human judges assess controversial COVID-19 and climate claims
